correspondence.component_scope: Chosen eastern opening and upper San Benito River
correspondence.finding: The selected eastern opening lies on the mapped upper San Benito River corridor in the Picacho Peak–Sawmill Creek Road surroundings. The connected channel runs west, turns south past the Union Carbide Road and Fawn Spring surroundings, then bends northwest through Williams Hollow. Repeated San Benito River labels and the connected drawn channel establish this upper passage. The opening is not asserted to be the ultimate or officially designated river source.

correspondence.component_scope: Upper northwest reach and Hernandez Reservoir inflow
correspondence.finding: The named river continues northwest through the Picacho Creek joining setting, Nimrod Canyon, the Augustine Creek and Clear Creek joining settings, and Hernandez Valley. It enters the southeastern end of the waterbody labelled Hernandez Reservoir. The selected line follows this connected river-to-reservoir corridor; nearby springs, tributaries and Mail Trail Pond are not substitute names for the trunk.

correspondence.component_scope: Hernandez Reservoir passage and mapped outlet
correspondence.finding: The original map depicts the connected elongated Hernandez Reservoir, its southeastern San Benito River inflow, selected passage through the main waterbody, and a northwestern outlet into the repeatedly labelled San Benito River. The selected route then follows the river west through the McCoy Creek joining setting. This establishes the ordinary managed-waterbody connection, without claiming current reservoir extent, releases, gate condition or a presently free-flowing natural channel.

correspondence.component_scope: Post-reservoir San Benito bends and northward valley
correspondence.finding: Below the reservoir the mapped river runs west through the Rattlesnake Gulch and Lorenzo Vasquez Canyon surroundings, turns north past the James Creek joining setting and Blue Jay Splash, and continues through Devils Canyon and the Old Hernandez Road valley. The connected mapped channel and repeated San Benito River labels support the selected bends. The simplified selected line cuts individual bends and local banks but does not require a distinct unmapped through-transfer.

correspondence.component_scope: Middle San Benito River through the San Benito settlement
correspondence.finding: The selected river continues northwest past the San Benito settlement, Shields Canyon and Bosworth Canyon. It follows the mapped trunk through the Sulphur Creek and Willow Creek joining settings and the Airline Highway crossing, then continues north through the Stone Creek and Pescadero Creek joining settings. Dry Lake lies separately to the west of the selected corridor; it is not a selected lake passage or a name for this river.

correspondence.component_scope: Paicines and Tres Pinos joining corridor
correspondence.finding: The San Benito River remains a connected mapped channel through the Pescadero Creek junction and the Cienega de Los Paicines setting, west of Paicines. It continues through the Southside Road bends to its mapped confluence with Tres Pinos Creek, then northwest beside Ridgemark. Nearby storage and pond features are distinguished from the selected trunk. The Tres Pinos channel and its adjacent managed ponds are not an inferred alternate passage of the selected mainstem.

correspondence.component_scope: Hollister and lower San Benito River
correspondence.finding: The named San Benito River runs along the western side of Hollister, through the Union Road and San Juan Road crossings, then west along the base of the Lomerias Muertas hills. The map shows its continuous continuation past the San Juan Bautista surroundings toward US101 and the Pajaro River junction. San Justo Reservoir is separately mapped southwest of Hollister and is not traversed by this selected route.

correspondence.component_scope: San Benito–Pajaro confluence
correspondence.finding: The lower San Benito River crosses the US101 setting and joins the Pajaro River immediately to the west. The map depicts the actual connecting channels, with San Benito River on the incoming southern arm and Pajaro River on the trunk entering from the north and continuing west toward Chittenden. This is a supported tributary-to-receiving-river transition, rather than a scalar rename of San Benito River or an inference from shared basin membership.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower Pajaro River through Chittenden, Aromas and Watsonville
correspondence.finding: The selected route follows the connected Pajaro River west through River Oaks, Chittenden and the Pajaro Gap, curves around the Aromas surroundings and continues along the Santa Cruz–Monterey county boundary. The river passes the Coward Creek and Corralitos Creek joining settings and the southern side of Watsonville beside Pajaro, then crosses the Cabrillo Highway setting. Soda Lake, Anzar Lake, Lake Tynan, Harkins Slough and other nearby waterbodies remain distinct and are not substituted for the selected river.

correspondence.component_scope: Actual coastal terminal at the Pajaro River outlet setting
correspondence.finding: Below the highway crossing the mapped Pajaro River continues past Pajaro Dunes into the coastal river/slough water complex at the Sunset State Beach–Zmudowski State Beach boundary. The actual selected rendered endpoint lies on this adjacent coastal outlet setting. The map shows the river widening into the terminal waterbody and the connected Watsonville Slough setting; it does not establish a present-day open breach through the beach or an exact contemporary mouth position. The short straight model tail cuts a local bend and shore before reaching the coast. This is ordinary coastal-terminal correspondence, not an all-water straight-line or current ocean-discharge claim.

correspondence.component_scope: Chosen mountain-side opening and small feeder connection
correspondence.finding: The chosen opening lies in the mapped small-stream setting on the western side of Rocky Branch, immediately south of the Lower Stairs Brook label. Original cartography depicts a short intermittent feeder descending into Rocky Branch. The model first bends northeast and crosses the local slope more directly than the mapped feeder; this is a generalized initial shape within the same connected side-valley and Rocky Branch joining setting. The source establishes the feeder-to-Rocky Branch relationship at ordinary corridor scale, rather than validating the exact initial vertices. The feeder is left unnamed; neither the Lower Stairs Brook label nor Rocky Branch is assigned as a scalar name to the initial feeder. The opening is not asserted to be the ultimate source of Saco River or Rocky Branch.

correspondence.component_scope: Rocky Branch valley and Saco River junction near Glen
correspondence.finding: Repeated Rocky Branch labels accompany the continuous southeastward mountain channel and its eastward lower valley beside Rocky Branch Road, Jericho Road and Jericho. The original map depicts its junction with the Saco River near Glen and Cooks Crossing. The selected corridor then follows the Saco River east and south. Ellis River, which enters the Saco farther east in the Glen–Lower Bartlett setting, is a distinct tributary; the selected upper route does not follow Ellis River. Kittredge Pond and the nearby feeder brooks are separate features.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower Bartlett, North Conway and the Swift River joining setting
correspondence.finding: The connected, repeatedly labelled Saco River runs south through Lower Bartlett, Intervale and North Conway, past the Lucy Brook, Kearsarge Brook and Moat Brook joining settings. At Conway the map shows Swift River joining from the west and Saco continuing east. The selected turn is supported by the original channel and confluence, not merely the proximity of the Conway place label. Echo Lake, Pudding Pond and the lake south of Conway remain separate waterbodies and are not selected through-lake links.

correspondence.component_scope: Center Conway, Fryeburg and the northern-to-eastern bend
correspondence.finding: The selected channel continues east past Center Conway into Maine, turns north beside Fryeburg, passes Swans Falls and turns east through the Town of Fryeburg setting. Cartography distinguishes this connected Saco River route from the separately labelled Old Course Saco River loop west and north of Fryeburg. The selected eastern channel joins the downstream Old Course/Dead Lake wetland-channel setting and continues south across the US302 crossing. The current cartographic channel connection is visible; no historical diversion date, engineered operating state or name equivalence between all old and present courses is inferred.

correspondence.component_scope: Fryeburg pond-channel complex and Brownfield river corridor
correspondence.finding: South of the Fryeburg bend, the original map depicts an uninterrupted water-channel network through the wetland and pond complex. Saco River is labelled in the channel north of Pleasant Pond; the selected corridor follows the river along the western side of the connected Pleasant Pond setting and the eastern side of Lovewell Pond, then continues south past the Little Saco River joining setting. Kezar Pond and Dead Lake are adjoining northern waterbodies and Lovewell Pond is a connected side waterbody, not a replacement name for the selected trunk. The river continues through the Shepards River and Old Meadow Brook joining settings near East Brownfield, then past the Boston Pond, Horseshoe Pond, pond surroundings immediately north of Hiram toward Hiram. Only the visibly labelled Saco trunk and Pleasant Pond passage setting are assigned names here; neighbouring ponds retain their separate identities.

correspondence.component_scope: Hiram, Ingalls Pond, Great Falls and Cornish junction
correspondence.finding: The selected river passes Hiram and the connected Ingalls Pond widening, continues through the mapped Great Falls/Hiram Dam Road narrowing, then runs south past West Baldwin. The map depicts Ossipee River entering from the west beside Cornish and the Saco continuing southeast and then east. This establishes the meaningful river junction and the selected fragment seam in the West Baldwin–Cornish corridor. Ossipee River remains a tributary identity and is not the selected upper mainstem.

correspondence.component_scope: Cornish, East Baldwin, Steep Falls and East Limington
correspondence.finding: The connected Saco River bends east from Cornish through the Goulds Island and Halfmoon Pond surroundings, past East Baldwin Mattocks Station, then turns south at Steep Falls. It continues along the county-boundary river corridor to East Limington and receives Little Ossipee River from the west below that crossing. The original water features establish the river and confluence; nearby Horne Pond, Wards Pond and Watchic Pond are not treated as selected through-lake passages.

correspondence.component_scope: Bonny Eagle and West Buxton widened river reaches
correspondence.finding: Below the Little Ossipee confluence, the Saco turns east and then south past Bonny Eagle. Continuous mapped river water, intervening constrictions and developed crossing settings connect the wider reach to West Buxton and the river below it. Bonny Eagle Pond lies separately to the east; it is not the selected widened river reach. The source supports the ordinary through-water relationship without establishing dam operating states, present releases or a new formal reservoir name.

correspondence.component_scope: Bar Mills, Salmon Falls and Union Falls impounded setting
correspondence.finding: The river continues southeast past the Junkins Brook and Crockett Brook joining settings to Bar Mills, turns south through Salmon Falls, and broadens into the connected waterbody receiving Cooks Brook from the west. The selected passage remains in the main north-to-south Saco waterbody and leaves through the mapped Union Falls narrowing. The whole upstream river, broad waterbody and downstream connection are depicted continuously. Cooks Brook is the separate western tributary arm; no additional scalar lake or reservoir name is assigned, and no current release or control-structure operation is claimed.

correspondence.component_scope: Dayton river bends and Saco–Biddeford transition
correspondence.finding: Below Union Falls the labelled Saco River continues through the broad Dayton-side bends, past the Stackpole Creek and Sandy Brook surroundings, across the I95 crossing and into Saco and Biddeford. The map shows the connected channel and divided river water around Spring Island and Factory Island, followed by the downstream widening. The developed urban channel and its constrictions remain part of the mapped through-corridor; no hidden transfer is required.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower estuary and actual coastal terminal beyond Camp Ellis
correspondence.finding: The original cartography depicts continuous lower Saco water through the Cow Island, Mouse Island, Gordon Point, Halls Point, Chase Point and Chandler Point settings, then past Jordan Point to the mouth between Camp Ellis and Hills Beach. The actual rendered endpoint is in open coastal receiving water east of Camp Ellis. The long final model extension crosses part of the Camp Ellis shore/spit before reaching open water, whereas the depicted river mouth connects to the same coastal water just south of it. This is a generalized terminal extension, not an exact navigable channel or an all-water straight line. The continuously mapped river-mouth receiving-water relationship establishes ordinary terminal correspondence; no separate unproven waterbody connection is introduced.

correspondence.component_scope: Chosen western headward opening toward the upper Turbio corridor
correspondence.finding: The extreme western chosen opening and its southeastward connection into the upper Turbio drainage are not unambiguously traceable as one watercourse in the acquired originals. The historical raster exposes the border-and-mountain setting but does not supply the full selected headward link. The bounded Chilean hydrographic originals supply neighboring Correntoso, Horquetas and Mirta drainage, not the missing selected connection. APN Map7 depicts the broader Turbio tributary network and glacial-source context, but does not resolve this precise chosen opening. This is a material source-correspondence gap, not proof of a nonexistent river, a formal boundary error, or an exact-bank mismatch.

correspondence.component_scope: Upper southern drainage and Río Turbio into Lago Puelo
correspondence.finding: The historical original depicts the eastward southern drainage, its northern turn, the Esperanza-side tributary junction and continuation into the Turbio valley. APN Map7 directly labels the receiving Río Turbio network and Map8 shows its lower channel and delta at Lago Puelo. These sources support the southern receiving corridor after the unresolved western opening. The APN hydrology section describes glacial sediment and meltwater contributions to Turbio; it does not establish a selected ice crossing or permit extending the Turbio name over the unresolved opening.

correspondence.component_scope: Lago Puelo passage and western outlet
correspondence.finding: The selected route follows the Turbio receiving lake northward and then its westward arm. APN Map8 exposes the Turbio inlet, continuous Lago Puelo body, and western Río Puelo outlet; its hydrology prose explicitly connects that outlet to the Chilean Lago Interior. The historical map independently depicts the same lake-to-outlet geography. The Chilean hydrographic feature at the outlet is directly Rio Puelo. This lake passage is preserved as a distinct waterbody rather than a uniformly named river.

correspondence.component_scope: Lago Interior and its northwestern Puelo continuation
correspondence.finding: The historical original labels L. Interior along the narrow Chilean receiving waterbody, while the APN original explicitly relates it to the Puelo lake outlet. The wetland inventory supplies the continuous lake polygon and the hydrographic original supplies the adjoining Puelo reaches. The separately mapped Lago de las Rocas is adjacent to the subsequent river corridor and is not imposed on this selected lake passage.

correspondence.component_scope: Río Puelo below Lago Interior through the Ventisquero and Negro receiving corridor to Manso
correspondence.finding: The complete hydrographic original directly names Puelo from the lake exit northward, maps the Ventisquero-side convergence, the intervening river corridor, the separate Negro and Alerce joins, and the lower bends to the Manso confluence. All selected intervening parts were inspected. Inventory riverine polygons corroborate the broad water corridor; neighboring Lago Azul and Lago de las Rocas are not selected through-lakes. The distinct tributary names are not whole-system aliases.

correspondence.component_scope: Manso–Puelo receiving junction and Lago Tagua Tagua passage
correspondence.finding: The Manso branch meets the Puelo trunk upstream of the northwestward lake passage. The historical original names Lago Tagua Tagua, and the inventory supplies its continuous lacustrine polygon with hydrographic inlet and outlet reaches. The selected simplified line passes through that connected waterbody at ordinary corridor scale. Neither the lake name nor the Puelo name is assigned to every preceding component.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower Río Puelo bends and actual estuarine terminal
correspondence.finding: Direct Puelo features continue below Tagua Tagua through the northwestern and western bends, past the separate Puelo Chico joining reach, and to the actual selected ending in the Reloncaví receiving setting. The riverine inventory polygon and historical map expose the terminal connection. APN hydrology prose identifies the basin outlet as the Reloncaví estuary. No further offshore extension, present estuarine water boundary, discharge or tidal state is asserted.

correspondence.component_scope: Northern tributary: extreme feeder south of Lago Guillelmo
correspondence.finding: The original historical raster clearly locates Lago Guillelmo and the adjoining mountain/road corridor, but its generalized or obscured drainage depiction does not establish the complete selected feeder from the actual southern opening to the lake. The lake label alone is not a missing-connection proof. No Chilean service coverage is claimed for this Argentine headward interval. This second geographic gap remains within the same single material-pending result.

correspondence.component_scope: Northern tributary: Guillelmo, Mascardi and upper Manso lake corridor
correspondence.finding: The historical original exposes the selected Guillelmo lake reach, its northern connection into the southern Mascardi arm, and the westward Manso corridor in the Los Moscos–Hess lake setting, followed by the southward turn. Lake and river identities remain distinct. The source supports the regional lake-and-channel sequence; exact shore positions, every minor upper channel name and present lake levels are unverified.

correspondence.component_scope: Northern tributary: Manso through Steffen and the Argentine westward/border reach
correspondence.finding: The original raster maps the southward Manso corridor into the Steffen lake reach, the outlet returning south to the Villegas-side convergence, the westward Manso valley and the northwestward border reach. Each selected part in this sequence was inspected. The neighboring Lago Martín is shown as an adjoining waterbody; its name is not imposed on the selected Steffen traversal. At the Chilean entrance, directly named Manso features continue the same geographic course.

correspondence.component_scope: Northern tributary: Chilean Río Manso to its Puelo junction
correspondence.finding: Complete Chilean hydrography directly names the southward and southwestward receiving channel Rio Manso, including the de Los Morros, Tigre Chico, Tigre and Frío joining contexts, and its final Puelo confluence. The historical original independently depicts the same broad corridor. The source does not rename the upstream lakes or the unresolved Guillelmo feeder as Manso.

correspondence.finding: The northern excursion and return are present in the selected path, but their river or lake continuity and meaningful junctions were not observed in a usable original source. Model adjacency is not substituted for that evidence.
